title: Tenali Raman Tale 76

full_text:
During a freezing winter in Vijayanagara, King Krishnadevaraya announced a royal challenge from his palace balcony:
'If any poor man can stand chest-deep in the icy cold waters of the palace lake from sunset until dawn, he shall receive a reward of five hundred gold coins and a fertile estate!'

A destitute young weaver named Deva, desperate to buy medicine for his ailing mother and food for his hungry children, accepted the perilous wager.
All through the freezing winter night, with northern winds howling across the lake, Deva stood shivering in the dark, icy water. Whenever his teeth chattered and his limbs grew numb, he fixed his eyes upon a solitary oil lamp glowing gently in a high window of the royal palace two miles away, drawing mental strength from the distant speck of light.
At sunrise, Deva emerged from the lake, blue with cold but alive and victorious!

Deva knelt before King Krishnadevaraya to claim his reward.
The King was about to hand over the gold when an envious courtier whispered:
'Maharaj! The weaver cheated! He confessed that he watched the warm glow of the palace lamp all night! He was warmed by the royal fire!'

King Krishnadevaraya, swayed by the courtier's sophistry, declared:
'Thou hast violated the wager! Thou wert warmed by the heat of the palace lamp! Thou shalt receive no gold!'
Deva was driven out of the palace, weeping in utter despair.

Tenali Raman heard of this cruel injustice.
The next morning, the King invited Tenali to a morning council, but Tenali did not arrive.
Hours passed; noon came, and still Tenali was absent.
Curious, the King rode to Tenali’s house with his courtiers.

In the backyard, the King found Tenali sitting under an ancient banyan tree.
On the ground, Tenali had kindled a tiny fire of dry twigs.
Tied to the highest branch of the banyan tree—forty feet up in the air—hung a small clay cooking pot containing water and rice!

The King stared in disbelief:
'Tenali! What madness is this? Thou hast placed a fire on the grass and hung thy rice pot forty feet up in a tree! How can the rice ever cook?'

Tenali looked up with innocent sincerity:
'Why not, Your Majesty?
If a poor weaver standing two miles away in an icy lake can be thoroughly warmed by the faint light of an oil lamp in a distant palace window, surely my rice pot forty feet above this fire will be cooked in an instant!'

King Krishnadevaraya stood frozen. The biting truth of Tenali’s demonstration struck his heart with overwhelming force.
The King felt deep remorse for his thoughtless cruelty.
He immediately summoned Deva, handed him one thousand gold coins—double the promised reward—along with royal robes of honor, and dismissed the envious courtier from court.
The people cheered Tenali Raman, who used an impossible cooking pot to deliver justice to the poor.
moral: Unreasonable royal judgments that deny rightful rewards must be mirrored by equally absurd logic to awaken conscience.
